techniques.name: 1. Separate the scroll target from the rendered progress (critically damped smooth-damp with a speed cap and catch-up)
techniques.problem_solved: Fixes the car from the previous project, which was tied 1:1 to scrollY. Every wheel tick, trackpad fling, scrollbar drag or End-key press turned straight into world-space velocity or a teleport, so the car moved too fast to follow and looked jerky.
techniques.how: Keep two values. TARGET is the raw scroll intent: read lenis.targetScroll (not animatedScroll, which would smooth twice), turn it into a 'chapter' float anchored on the DOM section centres, then pass it through a station map with holds so the subject parks while the copy is read. RENDERED is owned by the 3D layer. Each useFrame advances it with maath easing.damp, a Unity-SmoothDamp-style critically damped second-order spring. Because velocity stays continuous, it accelerates and settles without overshoot, and it is frame-rate independent. Its built-in maxSpeed argument caps speed. Express the cap in world units per second along an arc-length-parametrised curve: maxSpeed_progress = maxWorldSpeed / curve.getLength(), then use getPointAt/getTangentAt so speed is constant whatever the control-point spacing. Add catch-up: when the gap between target and rendered is large (the user jumped to the footer), raise maxSpeed in proportion, or do a fade-cut above about 35%, so the car does not crawl for 10 seconds. The subject and the camera use different damping. The car steers with dampLookAt (0.10-0.15 s). The chase camera uses a lazier damp3 (0.5-0.7 s) and looks at a damped point 2-3 units ahead. The car therefore drifts a little inside the frame, and speed is read from the world passing by rather than from the car darting across the screen. Clamp dt to 1/20 s or less, allocate scratch vectors once, and never call setState in the loop.
techniques.mobile_notes: On phones use about 0.8x maxWorldSpeed and add 0.1 s to smoothTime. With touch on syncTouch:false, the 3D damping is the only smoothing layer, which is what you want, because native iOS momentum stays intact. Damping is measured in seconds, so 60 Hz Safari, 30 Hz Low Power mode and 120 Hz Android all move at the same speed.

techniques.name: 2. Alternative: trapezoidal motion profile (limits both velocity and acceleration) for a vehicle feel
techniques.problem_solved: A spring starts moving the instant scroll begins. A car or train looks more physical when it pulls away, cruises at a capped speed and brakes into the station, and it never overshoots.
techniques.how: Each substep (dt split into steps of 1/120 s or less), compute the fastest speed that can still stop in time, sqrt(2*maxA*|d|), clamp it to maxV, and move the current velocity toward that desired velocity by no more than maxA*h. This gives a trapezoidal velocity curve: bounded acceleration, bounded speed and guaranteed no overshoot. Use it on the subject's u in place of easing.damp. Keep easing.damp3 for the camera so the camera still eases softly.
techniques.mobile_notes: It costs a handful of float operations per frame, so it is negligible on any device.

techniques.name: 3. One loop shared by Lenis, GSAP ScrollTrigger and R3F
techniques.problem_solved: Prevents competing requestAnimationFrame loops and stale reads. Without this, ScrollTrigger samples old positions, Lenis is ticked twice (jitter), loops pile up after Next route changes, and mobile FPS drops (Lenis discussion #431).
techniques.how: Use the official pattern: gsap.ticker drives lenis.raf(time*1000) (the ticker gives seconds, Lenis expects ms), set gsap.ticker.lagSmoothing(0), and call lenis.on('scroll', ScrollTrigger.update). In React, use ReactLenis root with options.autoRaf:false (the top-level autoRaf prop is deprecated) and reach the instance through a ref. Put the instance in a module store so the R3F useFrame can read lenis.targetScroll directly. R3F's own loop can stay as it is, because damping hides the one-frame ordering difference. For a strict single loop, run the Canvas with frameloop='never' and call advance(time) from the same gsap ticker, after lenis.raf. With frameloop 'never', R3F treats the timestamp as seconds, which is what the gsap ticker provides. This also lets you cap 120 Hz phones at 60 with gsap.ticker.fps(60) and stop rendering by skipping advance. Re-measure section centres on ScrollTrigger 'refresh' and after document.fonts.ready. Remove everything on unmount.
techniques.mobile_notes: Keep syncTouch false on iOS and Android. The README warns syncTouch is unstable on iOS below 16, it fights native momentum, and in #431 it removed the smooth feel. Lenis respectReducedMotion defaults to true. Safari is capped at 60 fps (30 in Low Power mode). Do not add a ScrollTrigger scrollerProxy when Lenis scrolls the window.

techniques.name: 4. Camera keyframes anchored to sections, on centripetal Catmull-Rom rails with holds
techniques.problem_solved: A global 0-1 page progress drifts out of step with the content once the sections have different heights, which they do on mobile because the copy wraps. It also gives monotonous, constant-speed travel.
techniques.how: Write one Pose (camera position, aim, fov) per DOM section [data-chapter], with separate pose sets for wide and tall aspects. Map the scroll position to a chapter float using the measured section centres. Damp the chapter with a speed cap (for example 1.2 chapters/s). Apply smootherstep(0.2, 0.8) inside each segment so the camera holds still while the copy is read and travels between sections. Run positions and aims through CatmullRomCurve3(points, false, 'centripetal'), since centripetal avoids cusps and loops. Use getPoint(t), not getPointAt: on an open Catmull-Rom curve, getPoint(i/(n-1)) lands exactly on keyframe i. Keep getPointAt for subjects that need constant speed. Use native CSS position:sticky for pinned chapters rather than ScrollTrigger pin, which avoids pin-spacer reflow, and never block wheel or keys, so there is no scroll-jacking.
techniques.mobile_notes: Choose the pose set by aspect ratio (wide or tall), not by user agent. On tall screens prefer moves in depth (dolly, crane, a 90-degree orbit) over sideways travel, and vary the move from chapter to chapter so it does not get monotonous.

techniques.name: 5. Stage architecture: one fixed full-viewport canvas behind server-rendered DOM (compared with drei ScrollControls and drei View)
techniques.problem_solved: Choosing a scroll and canvas architecture that keeps the copy server-rendered and indexable, keeps native scroll and accessibility, and still allows a continuous 3D world.
techniques.how: RECOMMENDED: a single position:fixed canvas (height 100lvh, pointer-events:none, aria-hidden) sits behind the real HTML sections, which stay in normal flow and are server-rendered by Next. Lenis scrolls the window. The 3D layer reads scroll from the store. Set eventSource to document.body (or a root wrapper) with eventPrefix 'client', so pointer and hover reach R3F while the DOM stays clickable. Pause rendering (setFrameloop('never'), or skip advance) once the 3D chapters have scrolled past, for example over the contact form and footer. drei ScrollControls builds its own scroll div in front of the canvas, and its <Scroll html> content renders client-side inside the canvas tree. That means no server-rendered copy, no window scroll, awkward anchors, find-in-page and scroll restoration, and a conflict with Lenis. It has damping and maxSpeed built in and suits self-contained experiences, not this company site. drei View cuts one canvas into scissored viewports that track DOM elements. Use it for small totems inside cards. Each view is its own scene render, adding draw calls, and post-processing applies to the whole canvas, so keep it to about four visible views.
techniques.mobile_notes: resize.scroll:false stops R3F re-measuring a fixed canvas on every scroll event. 100lvh means the canvas does not resize when Safari's toolbar collapses. Never use touch-action:none or OrbitControls on a full-screen canvas, because it blocks page scrolling.

techniques.name: 6. Premium-looking materials for colourful solid totems without extra render passes
techniques.problem_solved: A sculptural, lit, collectible look in place of flat drawn shapes, without paying for transmission on every object.
techniques.how: Base totems on MeshPhysicalMaterial with clearcoat (glossy lacquer), iridescence (oil-slick colour shift) and sheen (velvet edges). These only add shader math, with no extra passes. Bake several colours into one merged mesh with vertexColors, which keeps each totem to one draw call. Transmission is the expensive feature. three's built-in transmission re-renders the opaque scene into a render target; recent three exposes renderer.transmissionResolutionScale. drei MeshTransmissionMaterial renders another pass per material instance unless the buffer is shared, and backside doubles that. Reserve it for one hero glass piece and step it down by tier: full (samples 6, resolution 512, backside) on desktop; samples 3, resolution 256 and transmissionSampler (shares three's buffer) on tier 2; and fake glass (physical material with high clearcoat, iridescence and env intensity, no transmission) on tier 1. Make bloom selective: emissive parts with toneMapped={false} and a luminance threshold of about 1.
techniques.mobile_notes: Tier 1 and 2 phones get no backside transmission and at most one transmission buffer. With roughness above 0, a very small buffer still looks right (the drei docs suggest down to 32x32). Iridescence and sheen are cheap, but test the shader count: keep it to roughly 10-15 unique programs.

techniques.name: 7. Environment built from Lightformers instead of HDRIs, plus pointer-driven reflections at near-zero cost
techniques.problem_solved: Studio-quality reflections and brand-coloured rim light without downloading a multi-MB HDR or depending on a CDN preset, which drei says is not meant for production.
techniques.how: Place <Environment frames={1} resolution={128-256}> around a few Lightformers: a wide warm key strip, two coloured vertical rims in brand hues (this is what makes reflections colourful rather than grey), and a ring for a specular highlight. frames={1} renders the cube camera once, so there is no per-frame cost and no network request. Do not animate the Lightformers (frames=Infinity re-renders six cube faces every frame). For movement driven by the pointer, damp scene.environmentRotation instead; that is a uniform change and costs almost nothing. Add at most one direct light for crisp highlights or specular glints.
techniques.code_sketch:
<Environment resolution={q.envRes} frames={1}>
  <Lightformer form='rect' intensity={3} color='#fff3e0' position={[0, 5, -2]} scale={[10, 2]} target={[0, 0, 0]} />
  <Lightformer form='rect' intensity={2} color='#ff4d8d' position={[-5, 1, 1]} scale={[2, 6]} target={[0, 0, 0]} />
  <Lightformer form='rect' intensity={2} color='#2de1c2' position={[5, 1, 1]} scale={[2, 6]} target={[0, 0, 0]} />
  <Lightformer form='ring' intensity={4} color='white' position={[2, 3, 4]} scale={1.5} />
</Environment>

function EnvSway() {
  useFrame((s, dt) => { easing.damp(s.scene.environmentRotation, 'y', s.pointer.x * 0.5, 0.6, Math.min(dt, 1 / 20)) })
  return null
}
techniques.mobile_notes: Use envRes 64-128 on phones. It is rendered once, so the cost is mostly VRAM. Pointer sway does nothing on touch; drive environmentRotation from scroll velocity instead.

techniques.name: 8. Grounding: accumulative, contact or blob shadows instead of real-time shadow maps
techniques.problem_solved: Floating objects without shadows look pasted on, while real-time shadow maps (especially point-light shadows, which cost six renders each) are too expensive on mobile.
techniques.how: For a static hero composition, AccumulativeShadows (temporal, 24-60 frames, with RandomizedLight inside) gives soft raytraced-looking shadows and ambient occlusion, and costs nothing once the frames have accumulated. For totems that move, use ContactShadows with frames={1} once the layout settles (one depth render plus blur), or a cheap radial-gradient blob plane under each totem, scaled and faded by height. Avoid castShadow and shadow maps on mobile. If you do use them on desktop, keep the map at 1024 or below and turn off autoUpdate when nothing moves.
techniques.code_sketch:
<AccumulativeShadows temporal frames={q.tier >= 3 ? 60 : 24} scale={14} color='#3a2a55' opacity={0.8} alphaTest={0.75}>
  <RandomizedLight amount={6} radius={4} intensity={1.2} position={[4, 6, -2]} />
</AccumulativeShadows>

<ContactShadows frames={1} resolution={256} scale={12} blur={2.4} far={4} opacity={0.55} />

// blob shadow for moving totems
<mesh rotation-x={-Math.PI / 2} position-y={0.001} scale={1.6 - height * 0.3}>
  <planeGeometry />
  <meshBasicMaterial map={blobTex} transparent opacity={0.5 - height * 0.15} depthWrite={false} />
</mesh>
techniques.mobile_notes: Tier 1: blob shadows only. Tier 2: ContactShadows with frames={1}. Tier 3: AccumulativeShadows. All of them have near-zero per-frame cost once settled.

techniques.name: 9. Tiered post-processing stack (bloom, N8AO, grain, velocity-driven chromatic aberration, AgX tone mapping)
techniques.problem_solved: The film-like finish award sites have, without wiping out mobile frame rate.
techniques.how: @react-three/postprocessing merges consecutive effects into one pass (mergeMode 'auto', at most one convolution effect per pass), so noise, vignette and chromatic aberration together cost about one full-screen pass. Rough relative costs (profile on a real device): Noise/Vignette/CA are cheap and merged. Mipmap Bloom is moderate. N8AO is the expensive one: Medium is 16 AO and 8 denoise samples, halfRes is 2-4x faster for about 1 ms of upsampling, and the 'performance' mode is recommended for mobile. DOF is expensive; avoid it on mobile. Once you use a composer, set gl antialias to false and control MSAA with the composer's multisampling prop (default 4; 0 on mobile). Finish with a ToneMapping effect (AgX holds saturated brand colours better than ACES). Drive chromatic aberration from scroll velocity so it only appears in motion and settles to zero.
techniques.mobile_notes: Tier 1: no composer at all, and keep postprocessing in a separately dynamically imported module so it is never downloaded. Tier 2: Bloom, Noise and Vignette only, multisampling 0, DPR 1.25-1.5. Tier 3: add N8AO halfRes. Every full-screen pass multiplies fill cost, and fill rate is the mobile bottleneck.

techniques.name: 10. Device tiers, runtime PerformanceMonitor and DPR caps
techniques.problem_solved: One scene cannot hold 60 fps on both a desktop GPU and a mid-range Android phone; quality has to adapt without visible flicker.
techniques.how: Before mounting WebGL, check that WebGL2 exists, then run @pmndrs/detect-gpu v6 with self-hosted benchmarks (benchmarksURL; avoids the third-party CDN fetch and CSP issues) and combine it with navigator.deviceMemory and saveData. That gives tier 0 (poster), 1 (lite), 2 (mobile) or 3 (desktop). Apple GPUs are reported generically, so cap mobile results at tier 2. At runtime, PerformanceMonitor with flipflops={3} only steps down; onFallback locks to tier 1. Every tier change remounts effects and recompiles shaders, so allow only a few. Cap DPR at 2 on desktop and 1.25-1.5 on phones (many report 3+). On desktop only, you can call performance.regress() during fast scrolling with <AdaptiveDpr>; motion hides the lower resolution. On phones avoid continuous DPR changes, because each one reallocates the canvas and every render target.
techniques.mobile_notes: Target 60 fps on a mid-range Android phone at tier 2. Treat 45 fps as the floor that triggers a step down. On 90/120 Hz screens, cap rendering at 60 (gsap.ticker.fps(60) with the single-loop setup), or the GPU work doubles.

techniques.name: 11. Mobile composition: centred stage, setViewOffset framing and aspect-aware field of view (fixing the left-edge road)
techniques.problem_solved: In the tour-travel project the road ran down the left edge on mobile and felt monotonous. Phones need a centred, composed frame that still leaves room for the copy.
techniques.how: Move the world, not the subject: the totem or vehicle stays in a central stage zone and the path sweeps through the frame. On tall screens, recede into depth toward a vanishing point, or wind a helix or switchback around a vertical axis, so the curvature keeps changing. Use camera.setViewOffset to shift the projection centre without turning the camera. On phones the subject sits about 36% from the top with the copy over a scrim in the bottom 40%; on desktop the subject sits on the right third with the copy on the left. Keep the horizontal field of view roughly constant (derive the vertical FOV from aspect, clamped to 28-72 degrees), and when the clamp is hit, move the camera back through the tall pose set. Vary each chapter's move (dolly-in, orbit, crane up, cut to a new totem).
techniques.mobile_notes: Choose by aspect ratio, not user agent, so tablets and folding phones behave. Because the canvas is 100lvh, its bottom sits behind Safari's toolbar when the toolbar is visible, so keep the subject in the upper half.

techniques.name: 12. iOS and touch hardening, WebGL fallback and reduced motion
techniques.problem_solved: Mobile-specific failures: canvas resize jank when the address bar shows or hides, memory-driven context loss, scrolling blocked by the canvas, missing WebGL, and users who prefer reduced motion.
techniques.how: Make the canvas wrapper fixed with height 100lvh so it never resizes with the URL bar (repeated canvas resizes on iOS have caused memory crashes), set R3F resize {scroll:false} with a 150-200 ms resize debounce, and set pointer-events:none on the wrapper. Use the Canvas fallback prop to show <Poster/> when WebGL is unsupported, wrap the Canvas in an error boundary, and on webglcontextlost call preventDefault and swap to the poster. The poster is a lightweight AVIF of the actual scene with the same composition, which avoids layout shift. For prefers-reduced-motion: Lenis respectReducedMotion is true by default and falls back to native scroll. The 3D layer keeps the same chapters but uses held poses with a short damp (about 0.2 s), no idle spin or tilt, and no grain or chromatic-aberration flicker. Still render the totems; a static scene is fine.
techniques.mobile_notes: Do not use device-orientation tilt, because it triggers an iOS permission prompt. Use scroll-velocity lean instead. Keep text in the DOM, never as WebGL text, for accessibility and search.

techniques.name: 13. Loading in Next 16: client-only dynamic import, Suspense, a preloader that shows real progress, and shader pre-compilation
techniques.problem_solved: Keeps 3D out of the server render and the LCP path, avoids a fake progress bar, and removes the shader-compile hitch the first time each section's totem enters the frame.
techniques.how: next/dynamic with ssr:false must be called inside a 'use client' file; in a Server Component it errors. The server-rendered hero H1 and poster are the LCP elements, and the canvas fades in once ready. Inside the Canvas, wrap the world in Suspense together with <Preload all/>, which compiles and uploads off-screen objects too, and call gl.compileAsync(scene, camera) before revealing. drei useProgress only tracks loader-based assets (GLTF, KTX2, textures) via DefaultLoadingManager. Procedural geometry does not register there, so weight progress honestly: assets, fonts ready, shaders compiled. Self-host the Draco and Basis decoders. Under Turbopack (the Next 16 default), write GLSL as TypeScript template strings, or add a top-level turbopack.rules raw-loader for .glsl files.
techniques.mobile_notes: Detect the tier before downloading the 3D chunk, so tier 0 never fetches three.js. Also put postprocessing in its own dynamic chunk so tier 1 skips it. If you use a full-screen curtain, make its brand typography the LCP element and lift it after about 2.5 s regardless of progress.

techniques.name: 14. Asset strategy: procedural, merged, vertex-coloured totems (compressed glTF only when needed)
techniques.problem_solved: Large GLB downloads and many draw calls. The totems should be solid 3D sculptures that cost almost nothing to download.
techniques.how: Build totems from primitives in code: Lathe profiles (vases and columns), Extrude with bevel from SVG shapes (the logo mark), Torus, Capsule, RoundedBox, Icosahedron, plus vertex noise through three-custom-shader-material if wanted. Bake per-part colour into a vertex 'color' attribute and merge with mergeGeometries, which gives one draw call per multi-coloured totem. Scale the segment counts by tier. Use InstancedMesh for repeated decor such as particles, studs and road markings. Build geometry in useMemo, and split very heavy generation across idle frames. If a hero model is needed, run it through gltf-transform optimize with meshopt (decodes faster than Draco) and webp or KTX2 textures (KTX2 uses 4-8x less VRAM), with textures at 1024 or below on mobile. For drei useGLTF, pass a self-hosted Draco decoder path.
techniques.mobile_notes: Halve the segments on tier 1. Aim for 100k vertices or fewer visible and fewer than about 60 draw calls on phones. Procedural totems keep the whole 3D payload well under 1 MB.

techniques.name: 15. Interaction: cursor-reactive totems, magnetic hover, cheap hit-testing, and whether physics is worth it
techniques.problem_solved: Makes the site feel alive and tactile without tying up the main thread with raycasts or a 1.6 MB physics engine.
techniques.how: Cursor-reactive (cheap): dampE the totem's rotation toward state.pointer (normalised -1..1, available page-wide through eventSource). On touch, lean the totem with scroll velocity instead. Magnetic DOM buttons: GSAP quickTo on x and y, fine pointers only. Hit-testing: R3F raycasts every handler-bearing object on each pointermove, and with eventSource on body that is every mouse move. Attach handlers only to invisible low-poly proxies (material visible={false}) with raycast={meshBounds}. Pointer lighting: damp scene.environmentRotation (free) or move a single unshadowed point light; avoid animating Lightformers. Physics (@react-three/rapier 2.2.0, which pins @dimforge/rapier3d-compat 0.19.2; the compat package is about 1.6 MB gzip per bundlephobia): low value for a company site. Fake it with springs, or lazy-load a 'toybox' section on tier 3 with a fine pointer when it nears the viewport, and pause it off-screen.
techniques.mobile_notes: Turn off R3F pointer handlers on coarse pointers, or limit them to taps. Do not ship hover-only affordances. Rapier should never load on tier 1 or 2.

techniques.name: 16. WebGPURenderer and TSL decision: ship WebGL2 now, keep a migration path
techniques.problem_solved: Decides whether to build on WebGPU in October 2026.
techniques.how: three r186's WebGPURenderer with TSL is usable: it falls back to WebGL2 automatically, Safari 26, Chrome 113+ and Chrome Android 121+ support it, and Firefox Android does not. R3F v9 can host it through an async gl factory that awaits renderer.init(). But this project depends on WebGL-only pieces. pmndrs postprocessing and @react-three/postprocessing do not run on WebGPURenderer; WebGPU needs three's RenderPipeline (renamed from PostProcessing in r183). drei MeshTransmissionMaterial and Text (troika, onBeforeCompile) break, as does any ShaderMaterial or onBeforeCompile code. R3F v10, which is WebGPU-first with useRenderPipeline, is 10.0.0-alpha.5, and drei 11 is alpha and capped at react <19.3. Older iPhones fall back to WebGL2 anyway. Decision: WebGLRenderer, which is R3F v9's default. Keep custom shaders few and simple so a later port to TSL with R3F v10 is cheap.
techniques.mobile_notes: Performance of WebGPU on mid-range Android varies, and some scenes run slower than on WebGL. There is no mobile benefit for a scene of this size.

scroll_follow_solution:
Root cause in the previous project: the car's position was a pure function of scrollY. Every wheel tick, trackpad fling, scrollbar drag or End-key press became instant velocity or a teleport, and the camera moved in lockstep with it, so nothing in the frame was ever settled.

The fix has three layers.

(1) TARGET progress is the raw scroll intent. Read lenis.targetScroll in useFrame rather than animatedScroll; reading the smoothed value would stack Lenis's lerp on top of your own damping and feel mushy. Convert it to a chapter float anchored on the measured centres of the [data-chapter] sections (re-measured on ScrollTrigger 'refresh' and after fonts load). Then pass it through a station map using smootherstep(HOLD, 1-HOLD), so the subject parks while a section's copy is on screen and drives between sections.

(2) RENDERED progress belongs to the 3D layer. Each frame it advances with maath easing.damp(obj, 'u', target, smoothTime, dt, maxSpeed), a frame-rate-independent, critically damped SmoothDamp. Velocity stays continuous and it does not overshoot. Its maxSpeed argument is the speed cap, expressed as maxWorldSpeed / curve.getLength() so it means world units per second along an arc-length-parametrised curve (getPointAt/getTangentAt). Add catch-up: multiply maxSpeed by (1 + k*gap) when the gap passes about 0.15, or fade-cut above about 0.35, so jumping to the footer is not a 10-second crawl. For a more vehicle-like feel, swap in a trapezoidal motion profile (max acceleration, max velocity, braking speed sqrt(2*a*d)): it pulls away, cruises at the cap and brakes into the station without overshoot. Clamp dt to 1/20 s or less, allocate vectors once, and never call setState in the loop.

(3) Subject and camera are separated. The subject steers with dampLookAt (0.10-0.15 s). The chase camera has its own lazier damp3 (0.5-0.7 s) and a damped look-at point 2-3 units ahead, so the car floats a little in the frame and the sense of speed comes from the world passing by. Story beats such as a totem assembling or the lighting changing fire from RENDERED progress, so the scene never shows a beat before the subject gets there.

Lenis sync: one ticker. gsap.ticker.add(t => lenis.raf(t*1000)), gsap.ticker.lagSmoothing(0), and lenis.on('scroll', ScrollTrigger.update). ReactLenis root with options.autoRaf:false and syncTouch:false. For a strict single loop, use Canvas frameloop='never' and call advance(time) (in seconds) from the same ticker after lenis.raf; that also lets you cap 120 Hz phones at 60 with gsap.ticker.fps(60). On touch, Lenis passes native momentum scrolling through, and the 3D damping supplies the cinematic lag.

Starting values to tune: subject smoothTime 0.4-0.45 s, camera 0.5-0.7 s, maxWorldSpeed 12-16 u/s on desktop and about 0.8x on mobile, chapter-camera cap 1.2 chapters/s, holds of 20-25% either side of each section centre.
mobile_strategy:
1) Choose a tier before downloading WebGL. Check that WebGL2 exists, then run @pmndrs/detect-gpu v6 against self-hosted benchmarks, combined with navigator.deviceMemory and saveData:
- Tier 0: an AVIF poster of the real scene in the same composition (no three.js download).
- Tier 1: lite. No postprocessing chunk, fake glass, DPR 1.25 or less, half the geometry segments, blob shadows.
- Tier 2: phones. Bloom, grain and vignette in one merged pass, cheap transmission (samples 3, 256 buffer, transmissionSampler), DPR 1.5 or less, ContactShadows with frames=1.
- Tier 3: desktop with everything.
At runtime, PerformanceMonitor (flipflops 3) only steps down. Never flip DPR continuously on phones, because every change reallocates the canvas and all render targets.

2) Composition, fixing the monotonous left-edge road. Keep the subject in a central stage zone and move the world instead. Use separate wide and tall pose sets, chosen by aspect ratio. On tall screens, route the path into depth toward a vanishing point, or wind it as a helix or switchback around a vertical axis, so the road sweeps across the frame with changing curvature. Use camera.setViewOffset to put the subject about 36% from the top on phones (copy in the bottom 40% over a scrim) and on the right third on desktop (copy on the left). Keep the horizontal FOV constant (vertical FOV derived from aspect and clamped to 28-72 degrees) and pull the camera back on tall screens. Give each chapter a different move (dolly-in, 90-degree orbit, crane up, cut to a new colourful totem).

3) Scroll. Lenis with syncTouch:false, so native iOS and Android momentum is untouched and Lenis only smooths the wheel. The 3D layer reads lenis.targetScroll and damps it: about 0.8x speed cap and +0.1 s smoothTime on phones. Anchor chapters to DOM section centres, because mobile sections are taller.

4) Canvas. position:fixed, height 100lvh (no resize when Safari's toolbar collapses), R3F resize {scroll:false} with a 150-200 ms debounce, pointer-events:none on the wrapper, eventSource on document.body with eventPrefix 'client'. Never use touch-action:none or OrbitControls on a full-screen canvas.

5) Frame pacing. 90/120 Hz Android screens double the GPU work, so cap at 60 (drive R3F from gsap.ticker with gsap.ticker.fps(60)). iOS Safari already caps at 60 (30 in Low Power mode). Damping is in seconds, so perceived speed does not change.

6) Memory. Textures 1024 or smaller (KTX2 or webp), one transmission buffer at most, a small environment cube (64-128), and a webglcontextlost handler that swaps in the poster.

7) Touch interaction. No hover-only affordances. Totems lean with scroll velocity instead of following the cursor. No device-orientation, which prompts for permission on iOS. Magnetic effects only for (pointer: fine).

8) Reduced motion. Lenis respectReducedMotion (default true) gives native scroll. The 3D layer holds poses per chapter with a short damp, no idle spin, and no grain or chromatic aberration.

9) Layout. Tailwind 4 with 16px side gutters and no horizontal overflow. All copy is server-rendered DOM in min-h-svh sections. The hero H1 is the LCP element, not the canvas. Test on a real mid-range Android phone (Snapdragon 7-series class) and a non-Pro iPhone, not just the desktop emulator.
perf_budget:
FRAME
- Desktop: 60 fps (16.7 ms frame). Up to 120 on high-refresh displays only if the scene stays cheap.
- Mid-range Android (Snapdragon 7-series / Pixel 6a-7a class): steady 60 fps on tier-2 settings with the cap at 60. Below 45 fps sustained, PerformanceMonitor drops a tier.
- Low tier: 30 fps or more, otherwise the poster.
- Inside a frame: JS (all useFrame work, damping, matrix updates) 2-3 ms or less; GPU about 10 ms or less.

JAVASCRIPT (gzip; measured on bundlephobia today: three 0.186.1 ≈185 KB, @react-three/fiber 9.8.1 ≈57 KB, postprocessing 6.39.5 ≈113 KB before tree-shaking, gsap 3.15 core ≈27 KB, lenis ≈5.5 KB, motion 14.1 ≈48 KB full, rapier3d-compat ≈1.6 MB)
- Initial route JS (Next runtime + React + DOM page + GSAP/ScrollTrigger/SplitText + Lenis): 170-190 KB or less.
- Lazy 3D chunk (three + R3F + the drei parts used + maath): about 300 KB or less.
- Separate postprocessing chunk (r3f-postprocessing + postprocessing + n8ao): about 90 KB or less; tier 1 never loads it.
- Do not ship Motion and GSAP together on the marketing page.
- No Rapier unless lazy-loaded for tier 3 only.

GEOMETRY AND DRAW CALLS
- Mobile: 100k vertices or fewer visible (about 150k triangles or fewer); about 60 draw calls or fewer per frame, counting the extra scene pass from transmission and the post passes.
- Desktop: 500k triangles or fewer; 150-200 draw calls or fewer.
- One merged, vertex-coloured mesh per totem. InstancedMesh for anything repeated.
- 10-15 unique shader programs or fewer, all pre-compiled during the preloader.

TEXTURES, MEMORY AND LIGHTS
- Textures 1024² or smaller on mobile (2048² only for a hero asset on desktop), KTX2 or webp.
- Environment cube 64-128 on mobile, 256 on desktop, rendered once (frames=1).
- No real-time shadow maps on mobile.
- 2 or fewer direct lights plus the environment.
- Render targets: composer plus bloom mip chain plus at most one transmission buffer plus N8AO only on tier 3.

DPR
- Desktop: [1, 2].
- Phones: 1.25-1.5 (1.25 when post is on).
- Never native 3x.

NETWORK
- Total 3D payload: 1 MB or less on mobile with procedural totems, 3 MB or less on desktop.
- Hero poster AVIF: 120 KB or less.
- Fonts: 2 woff2 families, subset, 120 KB or less in total.
- Self-hosted Draco/Basis decoders and GPU benchmark data; no runtime CDN fetches.

CORE WEB VITALS (mobile)
- LCP 2.5 s or less (server-rendered hero text or poster, not the canvas).
- CLS 0.05 or less (the poster occupies the canvas box).
- INP 200 ms or less.
- Main-thread work from 3D initialisation (geometry build plus compileAsync): 300 ms or less in total, split across frames.

These per-effect costs and frame figures are starting estimates. Verify with renderer.info, stats-gl and Chrome remote debugging on a real device before locking them in.
pitfalls: Binding a 3D object 1:1 to scrollY (the previous car). Scrollbar drags and End/Home jumps become teleports. Always separate target from rendered progress and damp with a speed cap.
Smoothing twice: Lenis lerp plus 3D damping on animatedScroll feels mushy and laggy. Feed the 3D layer lenis.targetScroll and do the smoothing there.
Frame-dependent lerp (x += (t - x) * 0.1 per frame) runs twice as fast on 120 Hz screens and half as fast in iOS Low Power mode (30 fps). Use dt-based damp: maath easing or THREE.MathUtils.damp.
Not clamping delta. After a tab switch or a hitch, R3F's delta can be huge and objects jump. Clamp to 1/20 s or less.
A speed cap with no catch-up. Jumping to the contact section leaves the subject crawling for seconds. Scale maxSpeed by the gap or fade-cut past a threshold.

Using curve.getPoint for a subject that should move at constant speed (it speeds up and slows down with control-point spacing), or getPointAt for camera keyframes (it misses the keyframes). getPointAt is for constant speed; getPoint(i/(n-1)) hits Catmull-Rom keyframes exactly.
Uniform or chordal Catmull-Rom with uneven points produces loops and cusps in the camera path. Use 'centripetal'.
A global 0-1 page progress drives the poses, but sections have different heights on mobile, so 3D beats drift away from their copy. Anchor chapters to measured DOM section centres.

Calling setState or creating new Vector3/Color/Euler objects inside useFrame. That means React re-renders 60 times a second and causes garbage-collection hitches. Use refs, a mutable store and pre-allocated scratch objects.

Lenis + GSAP wiring mistakes: forgetting time*1000, leaving out gsap.ticker.lagSmoothing(0), running autoRaf alongside the ticker (double ticking), adding a scrollerProxy when Lenis scrolls the window, not destroying Lenis or removing the ticker on unmount (loops pile up after Next route changes), forgetting to import lenis/dist/lenis.css, or using the deprecated @studio-freight/lenis package.

ScrollTrigger pin combined with late-loading fonts or images and the canvas mounting produces wrong trigger positions. Call ScrollTrigger.refresh() after document.fonts.ready and after the stage is ready, and prefer CSS position:sticky for pinned chapters.

drei ScrollControls for a marketing site: its content is not server-rendered, it uses its own scroll container rather than the window, anchors, find-in-page and scroll restoration break, and it conflicts with Lenis.

Next 16: dynamic(..., { ssr: false }) in a Server Component throws. Put it in a 'use client' wrapper. Touching window or document at module scope breaks the build. Turbopack is the default, so .glsl imports need turbopack.rules (or write shaders as template strings).
React Compiler: stable but off by default in Next 16; the Rust version in 16.3+ is experimental. Do not enable it for the mutation-heavy R3F tree at first; use the 'use no memo' directive if needed.

iOS: a canvas sized with 100vh/dvh or tracked by ResizeObserver resizes on every toolbar show or hide. That causes jank, and repeated resizes have caused memory crashes. Use a fixed 100lvh wrapper, resize {scroll:false} and a debounce.
A full-screen canvas with touch-action:none, OrbitControls or pointer-events enabled swallows scroll and taps on phones. Put pointer-events:none on the wrapper and eventSource on body.

Continuous AdaptiveDpr or PerformanceMonitor flip-flopping on mobile reallocates the canvas and render targets each time and causes stutter. Set flipflops to 3, only step down, and use a fixed DPR cap on phones.
Leaving the renderer's antialias on while using EffectComposer wastes MSAA. Set gl antialias:false and the composer's multisampling (4 on desktop, 0 on mobile).

Tone mapping mixed up with postprocessing produces washed-out or double-tonemapped colours. Put a ToneMapping effect (AgX for saturated brand colours) last in the chain. Make bloom selective with emissive toneMapped={false} parts and luminanceThreshold of about 1, or everything glows.
Several MeshTransmissionMaterial instances each re-render the scene, and backside doubles the cost. Use one hero glass element, a shared buffer or transmissionSampler, and step it down by tier.

Environment preset in production fetches HDRIs from a CDN, and drei warns it may fail. Use Lightformers with frames={1}. Animating Lightformers (frames=Infinity) re-renders six cube faces every frame.
Real-time shadow maps or point-light shadows on mobile (six renders per light). Use AccumulativeShadows, ContactShadows with frames={1}, or blob planes.

Shader-compile hitch the first time a section's totem enters the frustum. Pre-compile with <Preload all/> and gl.compileAsync during the preloader, and keep the material set stable (no new materials or needsUpdate while scrolling).
A fake or looping preloader. useProgress only sees loader-based assets, so weight in fonts and shader compilation, and never block the server-rendered hero text that is the LCP element.

With eventSource on body, raycasting high-poly meshes on every pointermove eats CPU. Use invisible proxies (material visible={false}) with raycast={meshBounds}, and disable handlers on coarse pointers.

Version drift: postprocessing 6.39.5 caps three at <0.187 and R3F 9.8.1 caps react at <19.4, so pin exact versions. drei 11 and R3F 10 alphas are WebGPU-first and incompatible with React 19.3. @react-three/postprocessing 3.2.0, motion 14.1.0 and next 16.4.0 are only days old; keep 3.1.3 / 13.5.x / 16.3.8 as fallbacks.
Choosing WebGPURenderer now breaks @react-three/postprocessing, drei MeshTransmissionMaterial and Text, and any ShaderMaterial or onBeforeCompile code. Stay on WebGL2 for this build.

Mongoose 9 needs Node 20.19 or later, a higher minimum than Next's 20.9. Use Node 22 or 24 LTS. In Next, cache the connection on globalThis and use models.X || model('X', schema) to avoid OverwriteModelError during HMR.
Putting headings or copy in WebGL text (troika). It is not accessible or indexable, and it breaks under WebGPU. Keep all copy in the DOM and only decorative 3D in the canvas.

Treating prefers-reduced-motion as 'remove the 3D'. Keep the totems but hold the poses, drop idle spin, grain and chromatic aberration, and let Lenis fall back to native scroll (respectReducedMotion is on by default).

versions.next: 16.4.0 (latest, published 2026-10-06; previous stable 16.3.8). Requires Node >=20.9 and TS >=5.1. Turbopack is the default bundler. The React Compiler option is stable but off by default; the Rust React Compiler (16.3+) is experimental. middleware.ts is renamed to proxy.ts; params, cookies and headers are async.

versions.drei: @react-three/drei 10.7.9 (2026-09-25). Peers: fiber ^9, three >=0.159, react ^19. It still depends on detect-gpu ^5 for useDetectGPU. drei 11.0.0-alpha.7 needs fiber v10 and react <19.3, so it is incompatible with this stack.

All versions were checked with npm view on 2026-10-11. Other packages: maath 0.10.8 (easing.damp/damp3/dampE/dampQ/dampLookAt with a maxSpeed argument), @pmndrs/detect-gpu 6.0.26 (prefer it over drei's bundled detect-gpu 5.x; self-host the benchmarks), n8ao 2.0.1, @react-three/rapier 2.2.0 (pins @dimforge/rapier3d-compat 0.19.2; the compat package is about 1.6 MB gzip), babel-plugin-react-compiler 1.0.0, @gltf-transform/cli 4.5.1.

Compatibility: (a) the three <0.187 cap from postprocessing and the react <19.4 cap from R3F mean exact pins and checking peers before upgrading; (b) @react-three/postprocessing 3.2.0, motion 14.1.0 and next 16.4.0 are 1-5 days old, so pin them exactly and keep the previous patch as a fallback; (c) next/dynamic ssr:false must be in a Client Component.

WebGPU/TSL status (October 2026): three r186's WebGPURenderer with TSL is usable and falls back to WebGL2. Support: Safari 26, Chrome 113+, Chrome Android 121+ on Android 12+; Firefox Android has none. R3F v9 hosts it through an async gl factory with await renderer.init(). However, pmndrs postprocessing and @react-three/postprocessing, drei MeshTransmissionMaterial and Text, and any ShaderMaterial or onBeforeCompile code do not work under WebGPURenderer, and R3F v10 and drei v11 are still alpha. Decision: build on WebGLRenderer (WebGL2) now and revisit when R3F v10 is stable.
